title: Guessing when wrong answers cost
objectives: Decide when to answer, guess or skip when a wrong answer costs a point.

screens.prose: Some firms’ online tests score +1 for a right answer, −1 for a wrong one and 0 for a blank. A candidate’s sitting of 80 came back like this.
screens.question: What is the candidate’s net score?

hints.text: A wrong answer takes one mark away; a blank takes none.

feedback.correct: 62 right less 10 wrong: 52 net. The blanks score nothing.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take one mark off for each wrong answer, and none for a blank.

byKey.no-penalty: 62 counts only the right answers. Each wrong one takes a mark away: $62 - 10 = 52$.
byKey.blanks-too: You took the 8 blanks off too. A blank scores 0, so the net is $62 - 10 = 52$.
byKey.added: You added the wrong answers. Each costs a mark, so take them off: 52.

explain.text: Net is right minus wrong: $62 - 10 = 52$. Candidates report a pass band of about 50 to 60 net, so 52 is just inside. Whether those 10 answers were worth giving depends on how sure the candidate was.

screens.prose: Each bar is the average mark of a guess over many guesses, by how many options are left. Move the control to change what a wrong answer costs.

derive.caption: A wrong answer scores {{fixed(w, 2)}}. Each bar is a guess among the options left.

screens.question: Set a wrong answer to −1. How many options must be left for a guess to average exactly 0?

hints.text: Look for the bar that sits on the zero line.
With 3 left the bar is below zero.

feedback.correct: Two left: right half the time, wrong half the time, so 0 on average.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set the control to −1 and find the bar at zero.

byKey.three: With 3 left a guess averages $\tfrac13 - \tfrac23 = -\tfrac13$. Find the bar on zero.
byKey.one: With 1 left you know the answer: +1. The zero bar is 2 left.
byKey.four: A blind guess among 4 averages $-0.5$ at −1 a wrong answer.

explain.text: At −1 a blind guess averages −0.5, and $-\tfrac13$ after removing one option. Remove two and the guess is free. Now try −0.33 on the control: even a blind guess is free.

screens.prose: Each bar is an **expected value**: the average mark per guess over many guesses. With $k$ options left, a guess is right with chance $\tfrac1k$ and wrong with chance $\tfrac{k-1}{k}$. Weigh each mark by its chance and add.

state.caption: +1 right, −1 wrong: a guess among the options left.

screens.question: Some tests give five options. At +1 and −1, what is a blind guess among five worth?

hints.text: Right 1 time in 5, wrong 4 times in 5.

feedback.correct: $\tfrac15 - \tfrac45 = -0.6$: worse than a blind guess among four.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weigh +1 by $\tfrac15$ and −1 by $\tfrac45$, then add.

byKey.only-right: You counted only the right fifth. Four wrong guesses in five cost $\tfrac45$: $\tfrac15 - \tfrac45 = -0.6$.
byKey.only-wrong: You counted only the wrong four fifths. The right fifth earns $+\tfrac15$: $-0.8 + 0.2 = -0.6$.
byKey.four-options: $-0.5$ is the blind guess among four. Among five it is $\tfrac15 - \tfrac45 = -0.6$.

explain.text: The expected value is $\tfrac15 \times 1 + \tfrac45 \times (-1) = -0.6$. More options make a blind guess worse. Every option you remove moves the bar up.

screens.prose: Often you are partly sure instead of guessing: you think B is right, with a chance $p$ of your own. Answering then earns $p \times 1 + (1 - p)(-1) = 2p - 1$ on average. A blank earns 0.

state.caption: The bars fill as you type.

screens.question: Fill in what answering is worth at each level of confidence.

feedback.correct: Below half sure, answering costs; above half, it pays.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out $2p - 1$ for each row.

byKey.r0c1: At 40%: $0.4 - 0.6 = -0.2$. A blank beats answering here.

explain.text: Answering beats a blank exactly when $2p - 1 > 0$: when you are more than half sure. At 40% the blank is better by 0.2 a question. At 90% an answer is worth 0.8, not 1.

screens.prose: Candidates report the 80-in-8 test as forward only, with no skip. Q31 would take you 20 s to solve. Or you remove two options in 2 s and guess. Elsewhere you run at 6 s a question with 90% right.

state.caption: Solving Q31 at 90% right earns $0.9 - 0.1 = 0.8$ on average.

screens.question: You guess, then spend the 18 s saved on three more questions. What do the guess and those three earn together, on average?

widget.label: Average marks
widget.accept: 2.4: 0 for the guess, 0.8 for each of three.

hints.text: A guess after removing two averages 0.

feedback.correct: $0 + 3 \times 0.8 = 2.4$, three times what solving Q31 earns.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the guess, worth 0, to three questions at 0.8 each.

byKey.no-penalty: 2.7 counts 0.9 for each question. A wrong answer costs a mark, so each earns $0.9 - 0.1 = 0.8$.
byKey.all-right: That assumes all three are right. At 90% each averages 0.8: 2.4.
byKey.one: 0.8 is one question. 18 s at 6 s a question buys three.

explain.text: The guess averages 0 and the three questions 0.8 each: 2.4. Solving Q31 earns 0.8 in the same 20 s. So the trade gains 1.6, since 80 questions at 6 s use all 8 minutes.

screens.title: The follow-up
screens.prose: The interviewer follows up: “What if a wrong answer cost a third of a mark? Or nothing?” Rules differ between tests, so read the marking before question 1. Use the control to check your sums.

derive.caption: A wrong answer scores {{fixed(w, 2)}}. Each bar is a guess among the options left.

screens.question: Fill in what a blind guess among four is worth under each rule.

hints.text: Right 1 time in 4, wrong 3 times in 4.

feedback.correct: 0, $-\tfrac18$ and $\tfrac14$: the penalty decides whether a blind guess pays.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weigh the penalty by $\tfrac34$ and take it from $\tfrac14$.

byKey.r2c1: With no penalty a guess earns $\tfrac14$ and costs nothing.

explain.text: At −1/3 the penalty exactly cancels the chance of a right guess. With no penalty a guess earns $\tfrac14$, so answer every question. At −1/2 a blind guess still costs, though less than at −1.

screens.prose: You are stuck on Q47 of the reported 80-in-8 test. Two rules go round candidate forums: “never guess” and “always guess”.
screens.question: Which rule do you follow on Q47?

options.text: Spend a few seconds removing options, then pick one and move on
Leave it blank, so it cannot cost a mark
options.why: You chose never to guess. This test has no skip, so you must answer to move on; after removing two, a guess costs nothing.

options.text: Guess at once, without reading the options
options.why: You chose always to guess blind. A blind guess averages $\tfrac14 - \tfrac34 = -0.5$.

options.text: Solve it, however long it takes
options.why: Certainty costs time. 30 s on Q47 is five questions at 6 s, worth 4 marks at 90% right.

hints.text: What does a guess cost after removing two options?
The test is forward only, with no skip.
Remove options fast, then guess: the guess becomes free.

feedback.correct: Cut options, then guess: the guess goes from −0.5 to 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what each choice costs in marks and in seconds.

byKey.blank: You chose never to guess. This test has no skip, so you must answer to move on; after removing two, a guess costs nothing.
byKey.blind: You chose always to guess blind. A blind guess averages $\tfrac14 - \tfrac34 = -0.5$.
byKey.solve: Certainty costs time. 30 s on Q47 is five questions at 6 s, worth 4 marks at 90% right.

explain.text: Neither slogan is right. Each option you remove lifts a guess from −0.5 to $-\tfrac13$ to 0. With no skip the guess is forced, so make it as cheap as you can.

screens.prose: You weighed each mark by its chance. With $k$ options left, $+1$ right and $-w$ wrong, $$E[\text{guess}] = \frac1k - w\,\frac{k-1}{k}.$$ At $w = 1$ that is $\tfrac{2-k}{k}$. Answering at confidence $p$ earns $p - (1 - p)\,w$, so answer when $p > \tfrac{w}{1+w}$: more than half sure at −1, more than a quarter sure at −1/3.
screens.question: A test gives five options and scores +1 and −1. You remove two. What is a guess among the rest worth?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the options left, then use $\tfrac{2-k}{k}$.

byKey.free: Removing two makes a guess free only among four. Here three are left: $-\tfrac13$.
byKey.five: $-0.6$ is the blind guess among five. After removing two, $k = 3$.

explain.text: The formula needs the options left, not the options removed. Five less two leaves three, so $\tfrac{2-3}{3} = -\tfrac13$. A guess is free only when two are left.

screens.prose:
Some tests set the penalty so a blind guess is worth 0. Find that fair penalty $w$ for $k$ options.

1. Set the guess to zero: $\tfrac1k - w\,\tfrac{k-1}{k} = 0$ (the fair rule).
2. Multiply by $k$: $1 - w(k - 1) = 0$ (clears the fractions).
3. Solve for $w$.
screens.question: What is the fair penalty $w$?

feedback.correct: $w = \tfrac{1}{k-1}$: a third of a mark for four options, a quarter for five.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. From $1 - w(k - 1) = 0$, isolate $w$.

byKey.over-k: $\tfrac1k$ is the chance of a right guess. The penalty balances $k - 1$ wrong options: $w = \tfrac{1}{k-1}$.

explain.text: From $1 = w(k - 1)$, $w = \tfrac{1}{k-1}$. Four options give $\tfrac13$, the follow-up’s rule, and five give $\tfrac14$. Under a fair penalty a blind guess is free and removing an option makes it pay.

screens.title: Guesses and net scores in code
screens.prose: `guess_value(options_left, right=1, wrong=-1)` returns a blind guess’s expected mark as an exact `Fraction`. `net_score(answers, key, right=1, wrong=-1)` scores a sitting: `None` in `answers` is a blank and scores 0.

widget.how: Check runs 13 hidden tests, compared exactly. Eight are guess values as `Fraction`s, under four penalties. Five are sittings, one of them the first screen’s 62, 10 and 8.

hints.text: A guess is right with chance $\tfrac1k$ and wrong with chance $\tfrac{k-1}{k}$.
Return `Fraction(right) / k + Fraction(wrong) * (k - 1) / k`; in `net_score`, skip `None` and add `right` or `wrong`.

feedback.correct: Both functions match the bars and the first screen’s 52.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the guess value exact with `Fraction`, and let `None` score 0.

explain.text: `Fraction(wrong)` makes the sum exact, so $-\tfrac13$ is not 0.333... . In `net_score` the blank is skipped before the comparison, so it never counts as wrong.

screens.prose: Eight quick ones. Target: about 10 seconds each, 80 seconds in all. The app does not time you, so use your own watch.
screens.question: Fill in each answer.

rows: Expected net of 80 blind guesses, 4 options, +1 and −1
Accuracy above which answering beats a blank, +1 and −1

hints.text: Net is right minus wrong; a guess is $\tfrac{2-k}{k}$.
85% of 70 is 59.5; the rest, 10.5, are wrong.

feedback.correct: All eight. Note your time against 80 seconds.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Redo the amber rows.

explain.text: 70 answered at 85% nets 49, against 52 for the first screen’s candidate. Answering more only pays when each answer is more than half sure. Blind guesses at −1 drag the net down by half a mark each.

screens.prose: Before a negatively marked online test, write your rules on one card and keep it beside the screen. A rule you decided before question 1 is one you will not argue with at question 60.
screens.question: Select all that apply: which lines belong on your card?

options.text: Answer when more than half sure at +1 and −1; at −1/3, when more than a quarter sure
Remove two options, then guess: the guess is free
A question past 20 s: cut options and guess, then move on
Read the marking rule first: at the fair penalty $\tfrac{1}{k-1}$ or below, guess everything

options.why: This test is forward only with no skip, so you must answer. At more than half sure, answering pays too.

options.text: Guess blind on hard questions to save time
options.why: A blind guess costs half a mark on average. Two seconds to remove options makes it free.

options.text: Make up a slow question’s time later
options.why: Time spent is gone: a slow question costs the questions at the end.

hints.text: Keep the lines backed by a number from this lesson.
Three lines cost marks on average. The card is for this format.
The four correct lines: half sure, remove two, past 20 s, read the rule.

feedback.correct: Four rules, each worth marks: half sure, remove two, past 20 s, read the rule.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep each line whose average mark you worked out as 0 or better.

byKey.blank: This test is forward only with no skip, so you must answer. At more than half sure, answering pays too.
byKey.blind: A blind guess costs half a mark on average. Two seconds to remove options makes it free.
byKey.later: Time spent is gone: a slow question costs the questions at the end.

explain.text: Each line came from a number: $2p - 1$, the free guess with two left, the trade and the fair penalty. The three habits each cost marks. Warm up with the daily round from Today first, as for any arithmetic test.

ideas: At +1 and −1 a guess among $k$ options is worth $\tfrac{2-k}{k}$. That is −0.5 blind, $-\tfrac13$ after removing one and 0 after removing two.
At +1 and −1, answering at confidence $p$ earns $2p - 1$, so answer when more than half sure; at penalty $w$ the break-even is $\tfrac{w}{1+w}$, a quarter at −1/3.
A slow question becomes a cheap guess when the clock will end your sitting with questions unreached: 20 s buys a free guess and three questions worth 2.4, against 0.8.
summary.trap: “Never guess” throws away free guesses in a no-skip test; “always guess” blind costs half a mark each time.

quiz.prose: A sitting at +1 right and −1 wrong: 75 answered, 11 of them wrong, 5 blank.
quiz.question: What is the net score?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the right count first.

byKey.right-count: 64 is the number right. Take off 11 for the wrong answers: 53.
byKey.answered: 75 counts every answer as right. 11 were wrong: $64 - 11 = 53$.
byKey.blanks-too: You took off the 5 blanks too. Blanks score 0: 53.

explain.text: 75 answered with 11 wrong leaves 64 right. Net is $64 - 11 = 53$; the 5 blanks score nothing.

quiz.prose: A test scores +1 right and −1/2 wrong, with four options.
quiz.question: What is a blind guess worth on average?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weigh the −1/2 by the chance of a wrong guess.

byKey.full-penalty: $-0.5$ uses a penalty of 1. Here a wrong guess costs $\tfrac12$: $\tfrac14 - \tfrac38 = -\tfrac18$.
byKey.no-penalty: You left out the penalty. Three times in four it costs $\tfrac12$.
byKey.fair: 0 needs a penalty of $\tfrac13$. A half is more, so the guess still costs.

explain.text: Right 1 time in 4 earns $\tfrac14$; wrong 3 times in 4 costs $\tfrac34 \times \tfrac12 = \tfrac38$. The guess averages $-\tfrac18$, cheaper than at −1 but not free.

quiz.prose: A test allows blanks and scores +1 and −1. You are 55% sure that B is right.
quiz.question: What should you do?

options.text: Answer B: it earns 0.1 on average
Leave it blank: you might be wrong
options.why: A blank earns 0, and answering earns $2 \times 0.55 - 1 = 0.1$. More than half sure is enough.

options.text: Answer something else, since B may be wrong
options.why: Another option is less likely than B, so it averages below 0.

options.text: It depends on how many options are left
options.why: The options left set a blind guess. Your 55% already counts what you know.

byKey.blank: A blank earns 0, and answering earns $2 \times 0.55 - 1 = 0.1$. More than half sure is enough.
byKey.other: Another option is less likely than B, so it averages below 0.
byKey.depends: The options left set a blind guess. Your 55% already counts what you know.

explain.text: At $p = 0.55$, answering earns $0.55 - 0.45 = 0.1$ on average. Any $p$ above a half beats a blank. The margin is thin, so do not spend long on it.

quiz.prose: A section has no penalty for a wrong answer and four options. With 20 s left, six questions are unread.
quiz.question: If you guess all six blind, how many marks do you expect?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. With no penalty each guess earns $\tfrac14$.

byKey.blank: Blanks earn 0, but here a guess costs nothing. Each earns $\tfrac14$: 1.5 in all.
byKey.penalty: $-3$ uses a −1 penalty. This section has none, so each guess earns $\tfrac14$.
byKey.one: That is one guess. Six guesses earn $6 \times \tfrac14 = 1.5$.

explain.text: With no penalty a guess earns $\tfrac14$ and can lose nothing. Six of them expect 1.5 marks. Under such a rule, never leave a question blank.
